title: Scientists May Have Found a Lost Roman City
summary:
Along the Danube River in Austria, scientists may have found a whole Roman city that was lost for nearly 2,000 years.

Special scans found the city near the hamlet of Stein. It covered about 62 to 74 acres and had streets in a neat grid, like a modern city. Its biggest feature was an open-air theater that could hold about 8,000 people. The city was probably built next to an army camp around 80 C.E. People left about 100 years later. Nothing was destroyed, so they probably left in an orderly way.

Could this be Claudivium? That is a city named by Claudius Ptolemy, a writer from the second century. The new site matches the place he described. But no stone with the name Claudivium has been found, so scientists are not sure yet.

Archaeologist Mario Wallner and his team scanned the ground for three years. They found buried roads and about 640 coins.
why_it_matters: It shows children that real history can still be hidden underground, waiting to be discovered.

background_read: Roman cities had streets, theaters and army camps, and some of them were later lost as time passed.
Archaeologists study buried remains to learn where old cities were and how people lived there.
Special scans can show buried roads and buildings under the ground, helping scientists find a lost city.

WHERE: Along the Danube River in Austria, near the hamlet of Stein.
